extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, parties and counsel in PTAB inter partes review proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: A Patent Trial and Appeal Board Final Written Decision assessing patentability of challenged claims in an inter partes review, applying statutory law (35 U.S.C. §§ 102, 103, 112) and PTAB procedural rules. It sets out claim construction, legal standards, factual findings, and the Board's conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103 (KSR/Graham framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention. Apply the Graham factual inquiries (scope/content of prior art; differences between claimed subject matter and prior art; level of ordinary skill; objective indicia) and KSR’s flexible approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must show more than separate references that each disclose separate limitations — there must be a motivation to combine and a reasonable expectation of success. Obviousness requires that a person of ordinary skill would have selected and combined prior art elements in the normal course of research to yield the claimed invention (Unigene Labs.). Consider objective indicia (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others) when available. The inquiry is expansive and flexible (KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors / factual inquiries for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The obviousness inquiry is resolved based on underlying factual determinations: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address each factor; objective indicia can weigh against obviousness but must be tied to the merits of the claimed invention. The sequence of questions can vary, but the factors control the inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine prior art references
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness requires that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to combine references to reach the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation can come from the references themselves or from common sense/ordinary creativity if supported by the record (KSR). Mere possibility is insufficient; show why a skilled artisan would have selected the combination in the normal course of research and development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: For an obviousness combination, a person of ordinary skill must have had a reasonable (not absolute) expectation of success in achieving the claimed result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate predictability of the art; some unpredictability does not defeat obviousness. Use experimental results, prior art teachings, and expert testimony to assess whether success was reasonably expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors pertinent to determining the level of ordinary skill include: (1) educational level of the inventor; (2) type of problems encountered in the art; (3) prior art solutions to those problems; (4) rapidity with which innovations are made; (5) sophistication of the technology; and (6) educational level of workers active in the field (Envtl. Designs/Orthopedic Equip.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may define the skilled artisan as an individual or a team with combined skills (e.g., molecular biology/virology researchers working with protein engineers). Tailor the skill level to the technology and record evidence (expert declarations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (Phillips / 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms are given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention, looking principally to intrinsic evidence: the claim language, the specification, and the prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only construe terms that are in controversy and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (Nidec/Vivid). Use express definitions in the specification where present; dependent claims and specification admissions can inform construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to construe a term (Nidec/Vivid principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms need only be construed if they are in controversy and construction is necessary to resolve the controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary claim construction; construe specific terms (e.g., 'treating a coagulopathy') when their meaning may affect the outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of intrinsic evidence and specification admissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic evidence (specification, claims, prosecution history) is primary for claim construction and for assessing obviousness; admissions in the specification may be relied upon when assessing obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite and apply express definitions in the specification (e.g., definition of 'treat' in the patent). Admissions in the specification can support a person of ordinary skill’s expectations and may be used against the patentee (Koninklijke Philips).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of 'treating a coagulopathy' (case-specific claim construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent expressly defines 'treat' or 'treatment' as 'the prophylaxis and/or therapy and/or cure of this pathology,' and states therapy includes 'partial or total alleviation of the disease symptoms.' The Board construed 'treating a coagulopathy' to include prophylaxis and/or therapy and/or cure, including partial alleviation of symptoms, for any duration of therapeutic efficacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims (e.g., claim 16 reciting reduction/prevention of hemorrhages) can support a broader construction that encompasses partial symptom alleviation; absence of a duration requirement in the specification means duration is not required by the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement for § 112(a) and priority
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim the filing date of an earlier application (§ 119(e), § 120), the earlier application must disclose the claimed invention in the manner provided by § 112(a). The hallmark of written description is disclosure: the specification must convey to those skilled in the art that the inventor had possession of the claimed invention (Ariad; Lockwood).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written description requires more than what would render the invention obvious; it must show possession of the claimed subject matter as of the earlier filing date. General statements or desires are insufficient; concrete disclosure or examples are often necessary to support specific claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof required to claim priority (procedural/documentary requirements)
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on earlier foreign or domestic applications for priority, applicants must present the earlier application disclosure in a manner that satisfies §112(a) and provide necessary documentary evidence (e.g., English translations where required).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to provide English translations of earlier non-English applications during prosecution can undermine a priority claim; the record must show the earlier disclosure adequately supports the later-claimed limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written examples/data to support quantitative claim limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting quantitative limitations (e.g., expression levels, dosing ranges) require earlier disclosures that reasonably convey possession of those numerical ranges or show how to achieve them; mere general statements without examples may be insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of gene therapy examples or numerical data in earlier applications weighs against finding written description support for specific expression levels or dose ranges. Expert testimony may help, but cannot substitute for an earlier disclosure that conveys possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated if a single prior art reference discloses every limitation of the claimed invention (as of the relevant priority date); prior art published before the effective date is §102 prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the prior reference (e.g., Monahan) is prior art based on effective date/priority; compare specific claim limitations to the single reference’s disclosure. Where priority date is disputed, resolution of priority affects whether a reference is §102 prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range overlap and obviousness (In re Peterson principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior art disclosure results in values/ranges that overlap claimed ranges and the claimed ranges are not shown to be critical, the overlapping prior art can render the claimed ranges obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate overlap (e.g., prior art % of normal FIX expression overlaps claimed 'fold less' ranges). Absent showing of criticality or patentable distinction, overlapping ranges can defeat patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof in PTAB IPR final decision
rubrics_metrics.description: At final written decision, the petitioner must show unpatentability of the challenged claims by a preponderance of the evidence under 35 U.S.C. § 318(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board weighs the totality of evidence — prior art, specification disclosures, expert declarations, deposition testimony, and trial record — and issues a final determination addressing all claims challenged by the petitioner (SAS Inst.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and assessment of expert declarations and testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties may submit expert declarations and depositions to support factual assertions (level of skill, interpretation of data, expectation of success, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board evaluates credibility, consistency, and whether expert testimony is supported by documentary evidence. Expert testimony cannot substitute for missing written description in an earlier application; it assists in interpreting prior art and the state of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disposition of multiple grounds once a dispositive ground decided
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Board decides a dispositive issue and holds claims unpatentable on that basis, it need not reach other grounds of unpatentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite precedent (e.g., Gleave, Beloit). The Board may summarize alternative grounds but decline to decide them when not necessary for the final outcome.
